name: KeyStoreSpec
important_note: This is a CrySL typestate and argument-constraint rule for java.security.KeyStore—not proof that a keystore is hardware-backed, that a call succeeded at runtime, that key material is confidential, or that a provider-specific keystore type is insecure. The rule's whitelist contains only five type strings and is narrower than the set of types potentially available on Java or Android.

events.name: Get
events.condition: Observed when source/type resolution identifies java.security.KeyStore.getInstance(String) or java.security.KeyStore.getInstance(String, provider). It satisfies only the Get event; it does not establish that a provider supports the type, that the type passes the CrySL whitelist, or that the returned object was successfully used.

events.name: Load
events.condition: Observed when a resolved java.security.KeyStore receiver invokes load(InputStream, char[]) or load(KeyStore.LoadStoreParameter). It is protocol-valid only after Get on the same tracked KeyStore object. Observing the call does not prove normal return, successful integrity verification, successful unlocking, or that the keystore contents are trustworthy.

events.name: GetEntry
events.condition: Observed when a resolved java.security.KeyStore receiver invokes getEntry(String, KeyStore.ProtectionParameter). It is allowed only in the read branch immediately before GetKey, after Load, on the same tracked object. The call alone does not prove that an entry exists, is recoverable, or has an expected Entry subtype.

events.name: GetKey
events.condition: Observed when a resolved java.security.KeyStore receiver invokes getKey(String, char[]) and its result is modeled as the rule variable key. It is protocol-valid only after Load, optionally preceded by GetEntry in that repetition. The call does not prove that the result is non-null, that password recovery succeeded, or that the returned Key is private, public, or secret.

events.name: SetEntry
events.condition: Observed when a resolved java.security.KeyStore receiver invokes setEntry(String, KeyStore.Entry, KeyStore.ProtectionParameter). It is protocol-valid only after Load and must be followed by Store within the modeled write branch. Observing it does not prove that the provider applied effective confidentiality or protection to the entry.

events.name: Store
events.condition: Observed when a resolved java.security.KeyStore receiver invokes store(KeyStore.LoadStoreParameter) or store(OutputStream, char[]). It is protocol-valid in this rule only after SetEntry in the modeled write branch. Observing it does not prove successful persistence, durability, integrity protection, or that the output destination is access-controlled.

forbidden_inferences_without_evidence: Do not infer that a finding concerns android.security.KeyStore, AndroidKeyStoreSpi, javax.net.ssl.KeyStoreBuilderParameters, or another namesake type; KeyStoreSpec explicitly governs java.security.KeyStore.
Do not infer that java.security.KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore"), "AndroidCAStore", or "BKS" is inherently insecure merely because those strings are absent from this CrySL whitelist.
Do not infer hardware-backed key storage from use of java.security.KeyStore or from a type string such as "AndroidKeyStore" without Android Keystore/provider/runtime evidence.

Do not infer that a password is secure merely because its static type is char[]; the rule only rejects String-typed password flows for the three modeled password variables and checks notHardCoded only for passwordIn.
Do not infer that a load, getKey, getEntry, setEntry, or store operation completed normally from a statically observed invocation.
Do not infer that generatedKey[key, _], generatedPrivkey[key], or generatedPubkey[key] means the runtime Key is definitely non-null or has all three key roles.
semantic_scope: The rule observes selected factory, load, entry-read, key-read, entry-write, and store calls on objects resolved as java.security.KeyStore; it constrains the factory type argument and selected password arguments, then emits CrySL predicates for compatible traces. The representative class and method names alone do not establish that each finding resolves to this API type.

detector_semantics.claim: For a tracked java.security.KeyStore object, accepted use begins with a modeled getInstance overload and load overload, then repeats either an optional getEntry followed by getKey or setEntry followed by store. The type argument must be one of JCEKS, JKS, DKS, PKCS11, or PKCS12; passwordIn, passwordOut, and passwordKey must never be String-typed; passwordIn must not be hard-coded.
limitations: The raw rule does not model getInstance(File, char[]) or getInstance(File, KeyStore.LoadStoreParameter), even though these APIs return an already-loaded KeyStore.
The rule does not list setKeyEntry, setCertificateEntry, deleteEntry, aliases, containsAlias, or other documented KeyStore methods.

The rule's source does not identify a fixed detector release, configuration, classpath, Android API level, or provider implementation; behavior for unresolved calls and interprocedural flows depends on the detector implementation.
The CrySL source is referenced at the mutable master branch rather than an immutable commit.

documented_behavior: java.security.KeyStore is a provider-backed keystore API.

The documented getInstance(String) overloads create a KeyStore for a requested type; load initializes it; getKey recovers a key for an alias; getEntry obtains an Entry; setEntry saves an Entry; and store writes the keystore.
The Java API documents that getKey and setEntry throw KeyStoreException if the keystore has not been initialized (loaded).
preconditions: The provider must support the requested type for the selected getInstance overload.
For getKey and setEntry, the KeyStore must have been initialized/loaded.
A supplied load password can be used to unlock the keystore or check integrity; null may be permitted by the API, with provider- and operation-specific consequences.
A supplied getKey password must recover the entry where recovery is required; incorrect credentials can cause UnrecoverableKeyException.
setEntry requires non-null alias and entry; the protection parameter may be null.
unknowns: Whether CrySL comparison of the type argument is case-sensitive, normalized, or otherwise provider-aware is not stated by KeyStore.crysl.
The exact static-analysis definition of notHardCoded for derived, resource-loaded, encrypted, native, or callback-provided char[] values is not stated in this rule.
Provider-specific semantics for PKCS11, DKS, JKS, JCEKS, and PKCS12—including password handling and hardware-token behavior—are outside the rule.
The source rule does not state how exception paths, null returns, reflection, Kotlin delegation, or wrappers are modeled.

security_semantics.detector_claim: The detector rule claims compliant modeled API usage and selected static password/type properties, and it can generate inter-rule CrySL predicates after a compatible trace.
security_semantics.runtime_claim: The Java runtime documents initialization and provider/credential requirements, but does not make the CrySL whitelist or its hard-coded/String-flow policy a universal runtime security guarantee.

source_level: Resolve the receiver and static factory to java.security.KeyStore, not a project-local class or another framework's KeyStore.
Identify the exact invoked overload and, for getInstance, the type argument data flow.
Establish object identity/order across Get, Load, and subsequent modeled events.
For a constraint conclusion, establish the relevant argument flow rather than relying only on the presence of a method-name substring.
runtime: Confirm the selected provider exists and supports the requested keystore type on the deployed runtime.
Confirm that load completed normally and, where relevant, that integrity verification/unlocking actually succeeded.
Confirm getKey/getEntry result values, entry subtype, alias existence, and protection semantics if any of those facts matter.
For hardware-backed or Android claims, inspect the Android Keystore provider, key-generation/import path, KeyInfo/security level, and deployed device behavior.
compatibility: Check the target Java or Android API level and installed providers.
Check whether the application deliberately uses provider-specific types outside the rule whitelist, including AndroidKeyStore, AndroidCAStore, or BKS.
Check whether use of getInstance(File, ...) or unmodeled entry APIs is intentional and supported by the deployed JDK/provider.

known_false_positive_shapes: Android application code using java.security.KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore") where the static rule's five-value type whitelist is applied literally.
Android or provider-integrated code using "AndroidCAStore" or "BKS", which are absent from the raw rule's type whitelist.

Code using KeyStore.getInstance(File, char[]) or KeyStore.getInstance(File, KeyStore.LoadStoreParameter), whose documented behavior returns an already-loaded KeyStore but whose overloads are absent from the rule.
Valid code using documented setKeyEntry(...) or setCertificateEntry(...) instead of the rule's modeled setEntry(...).

Android application code that calls setEntry(...) on a KeyStore obtained with getInstance("AndroidKeyStore") without a following store(...): the Android keystore service persists an entry when it is set, and AndroidKeyStoreSpi.engineStore throws UnsupportedOperationException, so the rule's Store after SetEntry is neither needed nor possible.

A char[] password assembled from a literal, configuration default, resource, wrapper, callback, or native boundary where the detector's notHardCoded/data-flow approximation does not reflect the deployed secret-management controls.
Kotlin delegated properties, wrapper methods, reflection, or dependency injection that obscure the exact java.security.KeyStore receiver, overload, object identity, or call order.
unknowns: Which exact CrySL/CogniCrypt/CryptoAnalysis version produced the representative findings, and whether it used this current master-branch rule or a forked/versioned copy.
Which rule violation category corresponds to each reported message value of "unknown".
Whether every listed representative method actually reaches java.security.KeyStore through resolved bytecode/source types; the class and method names alone do not establish that.
Whether the detector treats unlisted KeyStore methods as ignored calls, protocol violations, or only incomplete evidence in the specific analysis configuration.
Whether String-flow and hard-coded-password detection accounts for all Kotlin/JVM compilation forms and Android resource/keystore integrations.

Whether the permissive generatedKey/generatedPrivkey/generatedPubkey predicates are consumed by other active rules in the analyzed rule set, and how those consumers interpret a Key returned by getKey.
non_security_violation_shapes: Android application code that reads a secret key with KeyStore.getEntry(alias, null) and KeyStore.SecretKeyEntry.getSecretKey() (or reads the same entry again with getEntry) instead of getKey(alias, password): the rule's read branch (GetEntry?, GetKey) admits getEntry only immediately before getKey, so the documented Android idiom leaves the automaton and is reported as an invalid call sequence. Both calls are read-only and return the same key from the Android keystore; no security property depends on their order. This shape covers only such reads; a sequence involving setEntry, store, or a missing load is not covered.
